content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published the second edition of its guidelines on aircraft disinsection methods and procedures. This document, available in both electronic and print formats, provides updated technical content and recommendations for controlling or eliminating insects in aircraft, baggage, cargo, and other areas to meet the requirements of the International Health Regulations (IHR) (2005). The guidelines emphasize that any use of the document must appropriately cite WHO and avoid implying endorsement of specific organizations, products, or services. If the document is adapted, the resulting work must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. Translations must include a disclaimer stating that WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation. The first edition of this document was published in February 2021 following peer review and consultation with experts and stakeholders. Feedback from users was incorporated into this second edition, which underwent further peer review in early 2023. The updated edition includes corrections and enhancements to the technical content. It also helps prevent the introduction of agricultural pests. The guidelines outline various disinsection methods, including pre-embarkation, pre-departure, residual treatment, and on-arrival disinsection. The document highlights the importance of integrated vector management, which involves rational decision-making to optimize resources for vector control. Effective vector control around airports can minimize the need for disinsection. Residual treatment, a long-term method, involves applying insecticides to aircraft surfaces to leave a persistent insecticidal deposit effective for up to eight weeks. Short-term treatments, such as pre-embarkation and pre-departure spraying, are designed to last for a single flight sector. The guidelines also address the use of specific insecticides, such as permethrin and d-phenothrin, which have been tested and recommended by WHO for aircraft disinsection. These products must meet national pesticide registration requirements, aircraft manufacturers' safety standards, and WHO specifications. The document provides detailed information on the application of these insecticides, including their residual and knockdown effects. WHO emphasizes that disinsection practices should be carried out in a manner that avoids injury or discomfort to passengers and crew. The guidelines also stress the importance of compliance with national and international regulations, as well as the need for periodic review of disinsection requirements based on current evidence and risk assessments. The document is intended for use by the airline industry, airport authorities, public health organizations, pesticide regulatory agencies, and other stakeholders involved in vector control and aircraft disinsection.
